naive forecast.simple: A forecast that repeats the last known value.

seasonal naive.simple: A forecast that repeats the value from the same point of the last season.
seasonal naive.example: Daily data, season 7: tomorrow equals the value 7 days ago.

drift forecast.simple: A forecast that continues the average change between the first and last values.
drift forecast.example: Values 10 to 13 over 3 steps give +1 per step.

mean forecast.simple: A forecast that always equals the average of the history.
mean forecast.example: History 10, 12, 14 gives 12 for every future step.

skill score.simple: One minus the model error divided by the baseline error. Positive means the model is better.

exponential smoothing.simple: A family of forecasting methods that use weighted averages where recent values count more.
exponential smoothing.example: Simple exponential smoothing, Holt and Holt-Winters.

level.simple: The current typical value of a series, with the noise removed.
level.example: Daily sales are around 50, so the level is 50.

smoothing parameter.simple: A number between 0 and 1 that sets how fast a smoothing method reacts to new data.
smoothing parameter.example: Alpha of 0.9 reacts fast. Alpha of 0.1 reacts slowly.

Holt's method.simple: Exponential smoothing with a level and a trend, so the forecast is a line.

damped trend.simple: A trend that shrinks by a factor phi at each step, so the forecast flattens.
damped trend.example: With phi 0.8 the extra growth fades away.

Holt-Winters.simple: Exponential smoothing with a level, a trend and a seasonal part, each updated with its own smoothing weight.
Holt-Winters.example: Daily sales with a weekly pattern and growth.

ETS.simple: A family of exponential smoothing models named by Error, Trend and Season type.

additive season.simple: A seasonal effect of constant size, added to the level.

multiplicative season.simple: A seasonal effect that is a percentage of the level.

autoregressive model.simple: A model that predicts a value from a weighted sum of its own past values.
autoregressive model.example: AR(2) uses the last two values.

moving average model.simple: A model that predicts a value from the mean and the last few random shocks. Not the same as a smoothing average.

invertible.simple: An MA model is invertible if it can be rewritten as an AR model of infinite order. Then the shocks can be estimated.
invertible.example: MA(1) with theta 0.5 is invertible. With theta 2 it is not.

ARMA.simple: A model that combines AR terms (past values) and MA terms (past shocks).
ARMA.example: ARMA(1,1) uses one past value and one past shock.

ARIMA.simple: A model with p autoregressive terms, d differences and q moving-average terms, written ARIMA(p, d, q).

SARIMA.simple: ARIMA with extra seasonal AR, difference and MA terms. Written SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)m.

AIC.simple: Akaike information criterion: fit quality minus a penalty for parameters. Lower is better, only for models on the same data.
AIC.example: AIC 402 beats AIC 410 on the same data.

BIC.simple: Bayesian information criterion: like AIC with a stronger penalty for parameters. Lower is better.
BIC.example: BIC prefers smaller models than AIC.

Ljung-Box test.simple: A test of whether residuals are white noise. A small p-value means leftover autocorrelation.
Ljung-Box test.example: p = 0.003 says the model missed a pattern.

recursive forecast.simple: A multi-step forecast that feeds each forecast back into the model as an input.
recursive forecast.example: Forecast tomorrow, then use it to forecast the day after.

maximum likelihood.simple: A way to fit a model by choosing the parameters that make the data most probable.
maximum likelihood.example: ARIMA models with MA terms are fitted this way.

Fourier terms.simple: Sine and cosine columns that let a regression learn a smooth repeating season.
Fourier terms.example: sin(2*pi*t/7) and cos(2*pi*t/7) for a weekly pattern.

changepoint.simple: A time where the slope of a trend is allowed to change.
changepoint.example: Growth slows down after a product matures.

dummy variable.simple: A column that is 1 when a condition is true and 0 otherwise.
dummy variable.example: 1 on holidays and 0 on all other days.

Prophet.simple: An open-source forecasting library from Facebook (Meta). It fits a trend, seasons and holiday effects.
Prophet.example: Forecast daily visits with weekly and yearly seasons.

intermittent demand.simple: Demand with many periods of zero and occasional sales of varying size.
intermittent demand.example: A spare part that sells once every few weeks.

Croston's method.simple: A forecast for intermittent demand: smooth the demand size and the interval between sales, and divide.
Croston's method.example: Size 4 and interval 2.75 give 1.45 per period.

SBA.simple: Syntetos-Boylan Approximation: Croston's forecast multiplied by (1 - alpha/2) to remove its bias.

TSB.simple: Teunter-Syntetos-Babai method: smooths the probability of demand in every period, so it handles items that stop selling.
TSB.example: The forecast decays during a long run of zeros.

ADI.simple: Average demand interval: the number of periods divided by the number of periods with demand.

hierarchical forecasting.simple: Forecasting many series that add up in levels, such as store, region and country.
hierarchical forecasting.example: Product sales sum to category sales.

coherent forecast.simple: A set of forecasts where the parts add up to the totals at every level.
coherent forecast.example: Store forecasts sum exactly to the region forecast.

summing matrix.simple: A 0/1 matrix S that turns bottom-level series into all series of a hierarchy: y = S b.

bottom-up.simple: A hierarchical method: forecast the lowest level and sum upwards.
bottom-up.example: Add up all store forecasts to get the country forecast.

top-down.simple: A hierarchical method: forecast the total and split it with proportions.
top-down.example: Country forecast times 30 percent for region A.

reconciliation.simple: Adjusting forecasts at several levels so that lower levels add up to higher levels.
reconciliation.example: Store forecasts sum to the national forecast.

MinT.simple: Minimum trace reconciliation: combines base forecasts using the error covariance so that the reconciled errors are small.
MinT.example: Often better than bottom-up at all levels.

overfitting.simple: When a model fits the noise of the training data and forecasts new data badly.

exogenous variable.simple: An outside input to a model, such as price or a holiday flag, that the series itself does not produce.

season length.simple: The number of steps in one repeating cycle.
season length.example: 7 for daily data with a weekly pattern.

baseline.simple: A simple forecast, such as naive or seasonal naive, that every new model must beat.
baseline.example: Repeat last week's value for each weekday and report the error of that rule.
